lines: Lecture three. Local search against population search, and how searches get stuck on hills.
Every evolutionary algorithm repeats the same loop.
Score everyone, then pick the fitter parents.
Mix two parents, then change one gene.
The child replaces the weakest. Then we repeat.
Visit every city once, then return.
A tour is a string. Add up the hops to get its length.
Shorter is better, so we minimise.
A B C E D is shorter. Twenty-eight beats thirty-two.
Five cities have only twelve tours.
Each extra city multiplies the count.
Twenty cities? We cannot check them all.
Start with one tour, and change it a little.
If it is worse, throw the change away.
If it is no worse, keep it, and carry on.
Repeat until time runs out.
Neighbouring solutions sit side by side.
Nearby solutions have similar fitness.
Hillclimbing climbs the hill it starts on.
It stops at a local peak, which may not be the best.
Here are four landscape shapes, with one climber on each.
Hillclimbing only ever walks uphill.
Only the one-peak shape always works.
Start from one solution.
Every solution one mutation away is a neighbour.
A different operator gives different neighbours.
Hillclimbing is stuck on this hill.
A worse step is usually rejected.
Let's fast-forward: every one is rejected.
Then, one lucky roll: it steps downhill!
Then it climbs on, and keeps the best.
Tabu search always moves to its best neighbour.
But it cannot step back onto a crumb it just dropped.
So it walks on, over the valley.
Both methods can escape the small hill.
One hiker is stuck on one hill.
A team starts on many hills.
Even a low score can climb the tallest hill.
The team gathers on the best hill.
And a team can select and recombine.
Remember: one loop, score, pick, change, and replace.
Hillclimbing stops on the nearest hill.
A team of searchers, or a lucky downhill step, helps you escape.
